claims.claim: The Crystal Palace models were the first dinosaur sculptures ever built.
claims.quote: The models were unveiled in 1854, as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world.

claims.claim: The building shown in studio.jpg is Hawkins's studio at Sydenham where he made the Crystal Palace dinosaurs.
claims.quote: Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins' studio in Sydenham, where he made the Crystal Palace dinosaur.

claims.claim: Hawkins modelled the animals full size in clay.
claims.quote: The dinosaurs were designed full-size and built in clay, from which a mould was taken allowing cement sections to be cast.

claims.claim: The models were unveiled in 1854.
claims.quote: The models were unveiled in 1854, as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world.

claims.claim: The studio photograph is by Philip Henry Delamotte and dates from 1853.
claims.quote:
Date: 1853
Author: Philip Henry Delamotte

claims.claim: Hawkins held a dinner inside the mould of one of the Iguanodon models on New Year's Eve 1853, to mark the launch of the models.
claims.quote: To mark the launch of the models, Hawkins held a dinner on New Year's Eve 1853 inside the mould of one of the Iguanodon models.

claims.claim: Guests sat at a laid table inside the standing Iguanodon.
claims.quote: Woodcut of the famous banquet in Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins' standing Crystal Palace Iguanodon

claims.claim: The banquet woodcut dates from 1854.
claims.quote: Date: 1854

claims.claim: Fifteen genera of extinct animals are represented, only three of which are true dinosaurs.
claims.quote: The sculptures represent 15 genera of extinct animals, only three of which are true dinosaurs.

claims.claim: The concept drawing (diagram.jpg) is Hawkins's own, dated 1854.
claims.where: Card 3 note and source; caption image list
claims.quote: Description: Concept drawing of Crystal Palace Dinosaurs by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins (1854)

claims.claim: The models were displayed on three islands acting as a rough timeline: Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
claims.quote: The models were displayed on three islands acting as a rough timeline, the first island for the Palaeozoic era, a second for the Mesozoic, and a third for the Cenozoic.

claims.claim: Megalosaurus was modelled as a four-legged (quadrupedal) animal.
claims.quote: Owen conjectured the animal was quadrupedal; palaeontologists now believe it to have been bipedal (standing like Tyrannosaurus rex).

claims.claim: Owen worked from a hip, a femur, a rib and a few vertebrae.
claims.quote: consisting mainly of a hip and femur (thigh bone), with a rib and a few vertebrae

claims.claim: The first suggestion that some dinosaurs were bipedal came in 1858, too late to influence the model.
claims.quote: The first suggestion that some dinosaurs might have been bipedal came in 1858, just too late to influence the model.

claims.claim: The geological island illustration dates from 1854.
Iguanodon's nose horn was actually a thumb bone.
claims.quote: lacking a skull, he conjectured that the thumb bone was a nose horn

claims.claim: Mary Ann Mantell found the Iguanodon fossil in Sussex in 1822.
claims.quote: Gideon Mantell sketched the original fossil, found in Sussex in 1822 by his wife, Mary Ann Mantell

claims.claim: The fossil lacked a skull.
claims.quote: lacking a skull, he conjectured that the thumb bone was a nose horn

claims.claim: Owen called the horn "more than doubtful", in 1854.
claims.quote: actually, even in 1854, Owen commented "the horn [is] more than doubtful"

claims.claim: The postcard used on card 5 dates from the 1910s.
claims.quote: Description: Postcard showing the Crystal Palace Dinosaurs from the 1910s

claims.claim: The sculptures still exist and have been Grade I listed since 2007.
claims.quote: The models were extensively restored in 2001, and upgraded to Grade I listed in 2007.

claims.claim: Funding was cut in 1855 after a total of £13,729 had been spent.
claims.quote: The building of the models however proved to be costly (totally £13,729), and in 1855, the Crystal Palace Company cut Hawkins's funding.

claims.claim: Half-finished models were scrapped.
claims.quote: Several planned models were never made, while those half finished were scrapped, despite protest from sources including the Sunday newspaper, The Observer.

claims.claim: A planned mastodon and a Dinornis were never completed.
claims.quote: Models of the "fearfully great bird" Dinornis of New Zealand (extinct by 1500 AD), and of the extinct elephant-like Mastodon (or Deinotherium of the Miocene and Pliocene of Eurasia and Africa), were planned for the 'Tertiary Islands' but not completed.

claims.claim: The card 6 postcard is titled 'Prehistoric Peeps' and dates from 1913.
claims.quote: CRYSTAL PALACE. PREHISTORIC PEEPS.

claims.claim: Hawkins built the models in a workshop in the park, then cast them in cement.
claims.quote: Hawkins set up a workshop on site at the Crystal Palace Park and built the models there.

claims.claim: The larger sculptures are hollow with a brickwork interior.
claims.quote: The larger sculptures are hollow with a brickwork interior.

claims.claim: Richard Owen provided the scientific direction.
claims.quote: The dinosaur sculptures, inaccurate by modern standards, were designed by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins under the scientific direction of Sir Richard Owen

claims.claim: An inaccurate map of the time is the only record of where the mastodon and Dinornis would have stood.
claims.quote: An inaccurate map of the time shows planned locations of the Dinornis and mastodon.

claims.claim: The models were Grade II listed in 1973 and extensively restored in 2001.
claims.quote: The models and other elements of Crystal Palace Park were classed as Grade II listed buildings from 1973. The models were extensively restored in 2001, and upgraded to Grade I listed in 2007.

claims.claim: The limestone cliff was blown up in the 1960s and rebuilt using 130 blocks of Derbyshire limestone.
claims.quote:
The limestone cliff was blown up in the 1960s.
In 2001, the display was totally renovated. The destroyed limestone cliff was completely replaced using 130 large blocks of Derbyshire limestone
